description:
Growing Food on Mars 🌱🔴

Hi! I’m Đức Anh, a Software Engineering student at FPT University, Vietnam. I build iOS apps and automated irrigation for my own farm. Our goal: grow food on Mars despite toxic perchlorate soil, using greenhouses, sensors and AI. A real problem NASA is still working on! Looking for: hardware, agriculture, AI/ML, data analysis & visualization, design, and Mars science. Curious? Join us!
summary: Coffee trees in Vietnam's Central Highlands are getting old, and farmers must pull them out and replant. Experts advise a 2-3 year rotation with other crops before replanting, so the soil can recover. Most smallholders farm on slopes, where bare soil washes away in the rainy season. ReRoot helps a farmer plan that gap. On a 3D map built from NASA SRTM elevation, the farmer clicks their hillside. ReRoot reads NASA data for that spot: slope from SRTM, plant cover from MODIS NDVI, soil moisture from SMAP, and 10 years of rain, temperature and root-zone wetness from NASA POWER. It scores five rotation crops (maize, peanut, soybean, mung bean and the green manure Crotalaria) against that climate. It then ranks every 2- and 3-year sequence with the farmer's own priorities: soil health, erosion control, income and water risk. Steep, rainy fields give erosion control more weight. The farmer gets the top three plans, each with a plain-English reason and the NASA numbers behind it.
details:
What it does: ReRoot is a decision-support tool for the 2-3 years between removing old coffee trees and replanting, built for smallholder farms on slopes in Vietnam's Central Highlands. A farmer clicks a spot on a 3D terrain map. The app shows the spot's elevation, slope, plant cover, soil moisture and average year of rain and temperature. It then recommends the three best crop sequences for the farmer's priorities and explains each one in plain English, with the NASA numbers behind it.

How it works: A Python script turns raw NASA files into small web data. SRTM 30 m elevation becomes 3D terrain tiles and slope. MODIS NDVI and SMAP L4 root-zone soil moisture become map layers. All of them go into a 200 x 200 cell grid (about 275 m cells) for a 55 x 55 km area of Dak Lak province. The grid, the crop table and a cache of NASA POWER answers live in a Postgres database (Neon) behind two serverless API routes on Vercel. The browser draws the 3D map with MapLibre on a Sentinel-2 cloudless base image. For each crop, the app finds the sowing month where the rain over the crop's season best covers the crop's water need (FAO values), and adds root-zone wetness. It ranks all 100 two- and three-year sequences with four priority sliders: soil health, erosion control, income and low water risk. Erosion risk (slope x months with 200 mm of rain or more) raises the weight of erosion control. A rain scenario (average, 30% wetter, 30% drier) shows how plans change.

Benefits and impact: Farmers see their own hillside and the reasons behind each plan, not a black box. Plans that start with dense ground cover and end with a nitrogen-fixing crop protect the soil during the rainy season and leave it richer when coffee goes back in. Extension workers can use the same view to explain options to farmers.

Factors considered: slope, heavy-rain months, rain in each crop's season, root-zone wetness, current soil moisture, plant cover, nitrogen fixing, organic matter, ground cover and income.

Tools and languages: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Node.js serverless functions, PostgreSQL (Neon), Python (NumPy, h5py, Pillow), MapLibre GL JS, Chart.js, Vercel, GitHub Pages. Code: https://github.com/Tlerd/Rotation-Planner-for-Coffee-Replanting

Creativity: ReRoot focuses on one real, under-served decision: what to grow while coffee is being replanted on slopes. It combines terrain, satellite soil moisture, vegetation and climate in one click, and every number shows its source.

Limits: Several crop values (sowing months, organic matter, ground cover, income) are still marked TODO and shown as unverified in the app. Scoring thresholds are the team's own simplifications. SMAP is one snapshot (31 Oct 2026) and NDVI one 16-day period (Oct 2026). Detailed data cover only the study area; elsewhere the app uses NASA POWER climate and a manual slope.

Use of AI: An AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic) helped with research, data processing scripts, code, the app and slide layout, and text. The team chose the problem and the approach, made the design decisions, reviewed and tested all code, and checked sourced numbers against their sources. AI-assisted files are listed in the README and in the commit messages of the repository. No AI-generated images are used; all images are screenshots of the live app.

SRTM GL1 v003 30 m elevation (SRTMGL1, tile N12E108)
SMAP L4 Surface and Root Zone Soil Moisture (SPL4SMGP v8, 9 km)
MODIS MOD13Q1 v061 NDVI 250 m (via ORNL DAAC MODIS web service)
projectRefs: Copernicus Sentinel-2 cloudless 2020 by EOX (ESA partner data, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
FAO Irrigation Water Management Training Manual No. 3 (Tables 6, 14: crop growing periods and water needs)
